list.listitem: The purpose of a sepsis evaluation is to identify infants who are at high risk for serious bacterial infections, so that they may be hospitalized and treated accordingly. B

Fever of unknown source in an infant younger than 60 days requires evaluation for an occult bacterial infection. This evaluation may include complete blood count, blood culture, catheterized urinalysis with urine culture, and possibly lumbar puncture. These tests may be used to stratify infants as high or low risk for serious bacterial infection. B
Lumbar puncture for CSF culture is necessary for infants 21 days and younger, but may be delayed in infants older than 21 days who meet strict low-risk criteria. A

Neonatal herpes infection should also be considered in infants up to 28 days and should be treated with IV acyclovir, if necessary. Evaluation for neonatal HSV includes HSV PCR of blood and CSF along with swabs of all mucosal surfaces and any skin lesions. A
See "Approach to the Patient" below for advice regarding evaluation of fever in well appearing infants less than 60 days of age, and for empiric antibiotic recommendations. A

Consider urinary tract infection (UTI) as a common source of infection in children aged 2 to 36 months with fever without source. In this age group, if patient is well-appearing and no source of infection is present, the use of empiric antibiotics in not recommended. B

This chapter will address the evaluation of the patient with fever without source in the 0 to 36 month age range with focus on 0 to 60 days. The newborn still in the nursery immediately after delivery is not considered here; for full evidence and treatment guidelines see specific reference.
Fever is defined as rectal temperature greater than or equal to 38°C.
Serious bacterial infection (SBI) is defined as a culture-confirmed pathogen in blood, spinal fluid, urine, or stool; new infiltrate on chest x-ray; or obvious bacterial focal infection.

In infants younger than 3 months of age presenting to primary care clinics with fever ≥38°C, UTI was present in 5.4%, bacteremia in 1.8%, and bacterial meningitis in 0.5%. This varied by age: 4.1% of febrile infants in the first month of life had bacteremia or meningitis, compared with 1.9% in the second month and 0.7% in the third month. Not all patients with positive CSF cultures had positive blood cultures.
Serious bacterial infections are present in approximately 10% of infants age 2 to 6 months who present with fever greater than 39°C.
The prevalence of occult bacteremia in febrile children aged 3 to 36 months is approximately 1.5% to 2%.
In contrast, fewer than 2% of well-appearing older infants and young children will be found to have bacteremia.
Neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection occurs in approximately 30 of 100,000 live births; 95% to 98% present before 22 days of life and only 7% to 14% present as fever without source.

Of children aged 1 to 36 months who presented with fever >38°C and with blood cultures performed in a community hospital emergency department, 3.5% of blood cultures were positive and more than 80% of those positive results were considered contaminants.

Common pathogens causing SBI in children ages 0 to 36 months include Escherichia coli, Group B Streptococcus (GBS), Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and other gram negative organisms.
Listeria monocytogenes is a rare cause of bacterial infections in infants, and mostly occurs in those younger than 2 months old.
Herpes Simplex Virus is also a cause of sepsis in infants younger than 28 days.
Serious bacterial infections in infants include UTI, meningitis, bacteremia, pneumonia, gastroenteritis, and other focal infections.
For information on specific pathophysiology of each disease process, see the chapters dealing with specific infections.

Screening and treatment for maternal GBS status using the CDC's guideline can prevent early onset neonatal GBS sepsis. This practice has likely resulted in a decreased incidence of GBS as well as E. coli sepsis in neonates. A
Vaccination against pathogens such as S. pneumoniae aids in prevention of disease.A
Prevention of sepsis in older infants and young children is accomplished by treatment against typical bacteria causing bacteremia, e.g. treating ear infections and sinusitis appropriately. A

Prophylactic IVIG in preterm and low-birth weight infants marginally reduces nosocomial infections (Risk difference: -3%; 95% CI: 0% to -5%; NNT = 33), but shows no decrease in mortality from infection. A

Diagnosis depends on combination of history, physical, risk stratification of patient, and lab studies. A Several sets of criteria exist to determine risk and treatment of febrile infants between the ages of 0 to 3 months (0-90 days) (i.e., Philadelphia, Boston, Rochester, American Academy of Pediatrics).
Infants 21 days old and younger with fever should have CBC, blood culture, a catheterized urinalysis and urine culture, as well as a lumbar puncture to obtain CSF studies and culture. C
Neonatal herpes infection should also be considered, especially in infants younger than 28 days. C

Fever in well-appearing infants aged 22 to 60 days requires the same evaluation as those younger than 22 days, except that lumbar puncture can be delayed or omitted if the infant meets low-risk criteria, there is inpatient observation or reliable outpatient follow-up within 24 hours, and family and physician are in agreement. C
All children younger than 1 year with fever without source A and girls aged 1 to 2 years B should be considered at risk of UTI.
Routine CBC and blood culture of well-appearing children aged 2 to 36 months with fever without a source is not recommended. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Positive CSF culture, CSF cell count, HSV PCR
Localization of herpes simplex virus from culture or polymerase chain reaction of CSF, surface swab, or blood
Diarrhea should be present, positive stool culture

list.listitem: Rule out sepsis evaluation occurs when an infant has a fever without a source after the history and physical examination.

Obtain rectal temperatures in infants who may have sepsis. Ear thermometers are unreliableand axillary temperatures demonstrate wide variability.However, subjective fever assessment by a parent is usually accurate.

Obtain an immunization history, especially regarding pneumococcal and haemophilus influenzae vaccination. Also determine key risk factors: preterm birth, hospital stay, maternal GBS, maternal chorioamnionitis, and maternal HSV status.

In acutely ill children in the primary care setting, physician opinion that "something is wrong", parent opinion that "illness is different from previous", cyanosis, impaired peripheral circulation, meningeal irritation, petechiae, and convulsions all greatly increase the likelihood of a serious bacterial infection. Other findings with relatively high positive predictive value for serious bacterial infection include unconsciousness, drowsiness, moaning, change in crying, decreased breathing sounds, tachypnea, and inconsolability.

On physical examination, the Yale Observation Scale for Infant Fever lists several positive predictors of SBI, specifically lethargy, poor or absent eye contact, failure of child to interact with parents or environment, poor perfusion, acrocyanosis, mottling, delayed capillary refill, and respiratory rate changes. Well-appearing infants and young children are alert, smile, are consolable, and are without signs of dehydration. Perfusion should be good with no delayed capillary refill, and there should be no sign of respiratory distress.
The magnitude of fever does not reliably predict illness severity, and response to antipyretics does not change the likelihood of serious bacterial infection.
The presence of febrile seizure does not significantly increase the risk of bacteremia in febrile children aged 2 to 24 months.
Infants younger than 22 days with fever should be presumed to have a serious bacterial infection.
Tachypnea is a sign of pneumonia and, when present, should prompt chest x-ray.
See "Approach to the Patient" below for AAP guidelines (2021) for evaluation of fever in a well appearing infant younger than 2 months of age.

After a good history and physical, as well as risk stratification (well-appearing vs. ill-appearing), ruling out a SBI generally includes diagnostic evaluations including the following laboratory tests: CBC with differential, blood culture, inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and pro-calcitonin, urinalysis, urine culture, and CSF studies including cell count, culture, gram stain, protein, and glucose evaluations. In addition, for localizing symptoms, tests for those specific regions are recommended (e.g., stool studies, chest x-ray).

Viral testing should be pursued if clinically appropriate. Viral testing could decrease hospitalization rates, specifically from influenza and enterovirus. Positive viral antibody testing does not eliminate the possibility of serious bacterial infection.

SBI is uncommon in children with bronchiolitis, but if SBI is present, UTI has been identified as the most common concurrent diagnosis vs. bacteremia or meningitis. (0-24 months, UTI incidence of 2.3%). SBI in the setting of RSV may be more common in high-risk patients and age groups. Testing for SBI in these cases should be considered accordingly.

Consider HSV infection in infants aged 0 to 28 days if risk factors are present or if the patient is not improving with antibiotic therapy. Often neonatal HSV infection will present with seizure, disseminated disease, or rash, although it can present with fever alone. Testing for neonatal HSV includes the following diagnostic tests: blood viral culture, CSF viral culture, CSF polymerase chain reaction for HSV, conjunctival viral culture, skin lesion viral culture, nasopharyngeal viral culture, rectal viral culture, and also consider liver function testing. Infants aged 29 to 60 days are unlikely to have HSV. Testing in this case should be reserved for infants with suggestive clinical findings or prior HSV infection.

Infants >2 months who are not critically ill and who do not require immediate antibiotics should be evaluated for UTI. Infants with a low risk of UTI with good follow-up may not require urine studies. In infants not in the low-risk group, send a catheterized urine for urinalysis and culture OR obtain a urinalysis first, and obtain a catheterized urine for culture if urinalysis suggests a UTI (positive leukocyte esterase, nitrite, or leukocytes/bacteria on microscopy). For girls, the probability of UTI increases to >1% with more than 1 of the following risk factors: age <12 months, absence of another source of infection, temperature ≥39°C, fever ≥2 days, or white race. Uncircumcised boys are not low-risk.For circumcised boys, the probability of UTI increases to >1% with more than 2 of the following risk factors: absence of another source of infection, temperature ≥39°C, fever >24 hours, or non-black race. Diagnosis of UTI requires urinalysis that suggests UTI (pyuria ± bacteriuria) and >50,000 cfu/ml of a uropathogen on a catheterized urine sample.

Obtain a chest x-ray in young children with fever without source and respiratory symptoms. A chest x-ray may be useful in children younger than 5 years with an elevated WBC count (>20,000) and a fever higher than 39°C without source.

For children aged 2 to 36 months with fever of unknown source who are well appearing, routine CBC and blood culture are not recommended. Children aged 2 to 36 months with fever who are not well appearing should have CBC and blood culture obtained. In children aged 2 to 36 months, a CRP test may not add diagnostic information beyond the WBC count and absolute neutrophil count, though there is conflicting information in the literature.

Patients with serious bacterial infection have higher average WBC count (>15,000), absolute neutrophil count, CRP levels, procalcitonin levels, and Yale Observation Scores than those without serious bacterial infections. Patients with CRP >80 mg/dl (LR+ 8.4; 95% CI: 5.1-14.1) or procalcitonin >2 ng/ml (LR+: 3.6-13.7; 95% CI: 1.4-25.3) are more likely to have a serious bacterial infection. Patients with CRP <20 mg/dl or procalcitonin <0.5 ng/ml are less likely to have a serious bacterial infection. A randomized trial found that restricting CRP to children with shortness of breath, fever of 40°C or higher, diarrhea, or where there was "physician concern" was safe. The utility of newer diagnostic tests such as cytokine and fibronectin levels has been explored but is not useful at this point.

Combinations of normal WBC, absolute neutrophil count, and procalcitonin results have a very good negative predictive value for ruling out bacteremia in infants aged 3 months to 36 months with fever and no obvious source. CRP and IL-6 are only moderately accurate, although normal IL-6 and normal CRP results have good negative predictive value (LR−: 0.07).

For children under 1 month of age, procalcitonin may also be helpful. It is less accurate in infants under 72 hours of age than in those 72 hours to one month of age. It should never be the sole or primary factor in a decision to treat.

Pediatric SIRS (systemic inflammatory response syndrome) includes meeting two or more of the following criteria (must include either temperature or leukocyte count abnormality): core temperature <36°C or >38.5°C, tachycardia (or bradycardia in infants), tachypnea, abnormal leukocyte count for age, or >10% immature neutrophils. Although children who meet SIRS criteria have an increased risk of needing to be admitted to the PICU, meeting SIRS criteria is a poor predictor of needing PICU admission (LR+: 2.74).
Febrile infants with +RSV studies have a decreased incidence of concurrent serious bacterial infections, with the exception of UTI.

The online Kaiser Permanente Risk Score estimates the probability of neonatal early onset infection based on maternal risk factors. A meta-analysis showed that use of the neonatal Kaiser early-onset sepsis calculator is associated with a decrease in antibiotic use (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.53 - 0.59) without an apparent increase in the rate of sepsis (pooled odds ratio 0.96; 95% CI: 0.26-3.52). This conclusion is tempered by a lack of randomized trials.

The PECARN Febrile Infant Rule was derived from a secondary analysis of 908 infants less than 60 days who presented to an emergency department with fever and validated on a second cohort of 913 infants. The rule uses the patient's urinalysis, ANC, and procalcitonin to identify a low-risk group of infants who could be managed without lumbar puncture or antibiotics. The clinical prediction rule had a sensitivity of 97.7% and specificity of 60% and negative predictive value of 99.6%.

The Step-by-Step approach to the febrile infant is another set of criteria developed by European emergency room physicians which uses urinalysis, urine culture, CBC, CRP, procalcitonin, and blood culture to identify a low-risk group of infants younger than 90 days who could be managed as outpatients without lumbar puncture or antibiotics. A recent validation reported that the Step-by-Step approach had a sensitivity of 92% and negative predictive value of 99% for SBI, compared with sensitivity of 81% and negative predictive value of 96% for the Rochester criteria.

The Lab Score is similar to the PECARN risk score in that it relies on UA, CRP and PCT. It was developed in 200 children at an Italian children's hospital age 7 days to 3 months old with rectal temp > 38 C as well as children 3 to 36 months old who appeared toxic or had a rectal temperature > 39.5 C. Given an overall risk of SBI of 23% in the validation population of 404 children, those with a low risk score < 3 points had a 5% risk of SBI while those with a score of 3 or higher had a 60% risk of SBI.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) Clinical Practice Guidelines (2021) utilize age, normal ANC and inflammatory markers to identify low risk infants with fever under 60 days of age who may forego lumbar puncture and/or undergo close observation as outpatients with or without empiric antibiotic therapy. Cutoffs for the biomarkers recommended below include ANC > 4000, CRP > 20 mg/L and procalcitonin > 0.5 ng/ml; see for low risk criteria. The AAP guidelines recommend:

For infants 8 to 21 days of age who are well-appearing: obtain urinalysis, blood culture, and lumbar puncture. May also obtain CBC with differential, CRP, and pro-calcitonin. Send HSV studies if there is risk of HSV. Initiate antibiotics and observe in the hospital.

For infants 22 to 28 days of age who are well-appearing: obtain urinalysis, blood culture, CBC with differential, CRP, and pro-calcitonin. If inflammatory markers are elevated, perform lumbar puncture. Lumbar puncture is optional if inflammatory markers are not elevated. If CSF reveals pleocytosis, is uninterpretable, or is traumatic, administer parenteral antibiotics and observe inpatient. If CSF is reassuring, empiric parenteral antibiotics may be given and observation may occur either inpatient or at home if follow-up is assured within 24 hours.

For infants 29 to 60 days of age who are well-appearing: obtain urinalysis, blood culture, CBC with differential, CRP, and pro-calcitonin. Lumbar puncturure should be considered if inflammatory markers are elevated. Infants with negative CSF results and those for whom lumbar puncture was not obtained may be eligible for an initial dose of empiric parenteral antibiotic therapy and outpatient observation if follow-up is assured within 24 hours.

For all infants 8 to 60 days of age, empiric antibiotics may be discontinued and, if hospitalized, the infant may discharge home if all culture results (and HSV results, if sent) are negative at 24 to 36 hours. See for recommended antibiotic regimens.
Infants 21 days and younger with fever are considered high-risk and should be hospitalized, lab studies completed, and empiric antibiotics given (see , ). A
Acyclovir should be administered to infants younger than 28 days who have fever without source and who are thought to be at risk of neonatal herpes. B

Infants aged 22 to 60 days with fever can be carefully observed as outpatients if low-risk criteria are met based on the history and diagnostic testing, and careful observation and follow-up is assured (see ). If the infant will be observed as an outpatient, consider empiric parenteral antibiotics prior to discharge. C
Ill-appearing children aged 3 to 36 months with fever without source should be treated with antibiotics after cultures are obtained (see ). C
See for empiric antibiotic suggestions based on age for treatment of infants 0 to 60 days with suspected sepsis. Once a specific pathogen is identified, antibiotic treatment should be tailored.
Add acyclovir when HSV is suspected.

Infants older than 21 days who meet low risk criteria (well appearing, no evidence of infection, normal laboratory results) can be carefully observed without giving antibiotics. While febrile infants aged 22 to 28 days not receiving empiric antibiotics should be observed in an inpatient setting, febrile infants who are 29 to 60 days may be observed outpatient without giving antibiotics if they meet low risk criteria.
All children with UTI, gastroenteritis, pneumonia, or other focal infections should be treated for the specific disease process.

In older children aged 3 to 36 months, consider empiric antibiotic therapy when they present with fever without source of 39°C or higher and with a WBC count of at least 15,000. Children with abnormal laboratory results that suggest a risk of bacteremia should be treated with antibiotics after cultures are obtained, but there is no clear evidence regarding which antibiotics are most appropriate, especially since the availability of a conjugated pneumococcal vaccine has significantly reduced the risk of pneumococcal bacteremia.

Gentamicin dosing in older children has been shown to be superior in one time daily dosing vs. multiple doses per day. A Cochrane review of 11 RCTs involving primarily infants >32 weeks showed insufficient evidence to conclude whether 'once a day' dosing versus 'multiple doses' per day is superior for treating neonatal sepsis. However, pharmacokinetic data suggests that 'once a day' dosing regimens are superior, as they achieve higher peak levels and avoid toxic trough levels. Therefore, the author concludes that, based on pharmacokinetic data, once a day dosing may be superior for treatment of sepsis in neonates older than 32 weeks.

Traditionally, ampicillin is added to the empiric antibiotic choices for a febrile neonate in order to treat presumed infections by Listeria monocytogenes and Enterococcus species. A recent meta-analysis has detected an epidemiologic change in the pathogens causing SBI in infants ≤90 days with fever. The conclusion of this analysis is that SBI caused by L. monocytogenes or Enterococcus spp. is rare in infants with fever. Based on this finding, the authors suggest that clinicians consider a change in the choice of empiric antibiotic coverage.
Ibuprofen, in children >6 months, may have marginally greater effectiveness for fever reduction than acetaminophen in a 1-time dose. There was no identified difference in safety.
Evidence does not support the use of IVIG in neonatal sepsis (mortality RR: 1.00; 95% CI: 0.92-1.08).
Overall evidence does not support the use of corticosteroids in severe sepsis and septic shock (28-day mortality RR: 0.87; 95% CI: 0.74-1.01).
Some infants may require fluid support, especially if they are receiving potentially nephrotoxic drugs.
Watch bacterial cultures for a minimum of 24 to 36 hours of incubation.
Empiric therapy is generally continued until culture results are known, then tailored on the basis of culture results.
Hospitalize febrile infants <22 days for observation and possible antibiotic therapy.

Low-risk infants aged 22 to 60 days may be observed as inpatients or outpatients, with or without antibiotics. See for low-risk criteria. These low-risk infants may be sent home with or without an initial dose of empiric parenteral antibiotics if they are available for repeat physical examinations at 24 and 48 hours. The patient's social situation must be considered.
Ill-appearing children should be hospitalized, cultured, and treated.
Untreated sepsis can be fatal. C
The prognosis of serious bacterial infection in children is dependent on the age of patient, location, infectious agent, and clinical course. C
All children with fever should be observed carefully and should be returned to medical attention if signs and symptoms worsen. C
A pediatric sequential organ failure assessment (pSOFA) score less than 2 had excellent negative predictive value for in-hospital mortality.B

algorithm.title: Evaluation of fever in infants up to 60 days of age

cell.label: Evaluation of fever in infants up to 60 days of age. Focal infection?
Well appearing (interactive, good perfusion, no respiratory distress or lethargy)?

Order lab studies: CBC, blood culture; UA and urine culture (catheterized or suprapubic tap). If not low risk (see Table 1), consider CSF culture and CSF studies. Additional studies if applicable: if tachypnea, CXR; if diarrhea, stool smear and culture.
CSF pleocytosis? If CSF not obtained, is the infant <29 days?
Secure follow-up within 12-24 hours (family and physician agreement)?

Obtain routine laboratory studies: complete blood count (CBC), blood culture; urinalysis (UA) and urine culture (catheterized or suprapubic tap); cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture and CSF studies (cell count, glucose, protein). Additional studies if applicable: if tachypnea, chest x-ray (CXR); if diarrhea, stool smear and culture. Give empiric antibiotics (Table 2). Hospitalize and observe until cultures remain negative for 24-36 hours. Consider herpes simplex virus for infants <28 days.
Give empiric antibiotics (Table 2) and hospitalize until cultures are negative for 24-36 hours.
Two options: (1) give IV/IM antibiotics (see Table 2) and observe at home, reassessing in 24 hours; or (2) give IV/IM antibiotics (see Table 2) and observe in the hospital.
Manage according to laboratory results, study results, and clinical course.

feature.caption: Low-Risk Criteria in Infants Younger than 60 Days.

tr.td: History
Well appearing, no evident source of infection, age > 21 days
Complete blood count
ANC < or = 4000 per mm3
Inflammatory markers
Procalcitonin <= 0.5 ng/mL, CRP <= 20 mg/L
Cerebrospinal fluid
No pleocytosis present, non-traumatic tap, normal protein, normal glucose, and negative Gram stain

feature.caption: Empiric Antibiotics for Healthy Appearing Infants with Fever Without Source.

tr.td: 0-21 days, UTI suspected
Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 8 hours PLUS either gentamicin 4 mg/kg IV or IM every 24 hours or ceftazidime 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 8 hours.
0-21 days, no focus identified, meningitis not a concern

Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 8 hours PLUS either gentamicin 4 mg/kg IV or IM every 24 hours OR ceftazidime 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 8 hours. If HSV suspected, add acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q 8 hours.
0-21 days, bacterial meningitis
Ampicillin IV or IM 75 mg/kg every 6 hours and ceftazidime IV or IM 50 mg/kg every 8 hours. If HSV suspected, add acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q 8 hours.
22-28 days, UTI suspected
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 24 hours.
22-28 days, no focus identified, meningitis not a concern
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 24 hours. If HSV suspected, add acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q 8 hours.
22-28 days, bacterial meningitis
Ampicillin 75 mg/kg IV every 6 hours PLUS either ceftazidime 50 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. If HSV suspected, add acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q 8 hours.
29-60 days, UTI suspected
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 24 hours. Consider oral medications if tolerated: cephalexin 50-100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses OR cefixime 8 mg/kg/day in a single daily dose.
29-60 days, no focus identified, meningitis not a concern
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 24 hours.
29-60 days, bacterial meningitis
Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg IV every 24 hours or divided every 12 hours OR ceftazidime 150 mg/kg/day IV divided every 6 hours PLUS vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day IV divided every 8 hours.
